extracted.intended_audience: computer science and mathematics students (authors of technical papers, proofs, and expository writing)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for clear, concise, and well-organized mathematical/technical writing, covering semantics, syntax, symbols, style, punctuation, proofs, and use of mechanical style-checkers. Aimed at improving exposition, proofs, and copy-editing for CS/math audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do organize
rubrics_metrics.description: Do organize material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organization means more than linear order; weave branches and alternative threads together, provide an anchor and a rough outline. Spend substantial time on organization; examine examples (thesaurus, encyclopedia, good textbook) for non-linearly organized presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distract the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not distract the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grammatical oddities, distracting notation changes, gratuitous stylistic quirks, and anything that pulls attention away from the content. If you want to jar readers, you may intentionally distract (change notation, use ungrammatical sentences), but usually clarity should prevail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use readability metrics cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs compute readability 'grades' from averages (words/sentence, syllables/word) via linear regression against subjective grade levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These automated scores are superficial but useful as a prompt to re-read prose. Aim to minimise grade level but don't overdo it; consider other parameters (sentence length distribution, POS frequencies, passive voice percentage). Treat program output as an aid, not arbiter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept machine suggestions judiciously (diction/explain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction flags a built-in list of questionable words/phrases; explain expands on diction's objections and recommends alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users reportedly accept about 50% of diction's suggestions. Be aware of domain exceptions (e.g., mathematical 'due to') and keep automated tools 'in their place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness / cut unnecessary phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise; cut whole phrases that do not add meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remove 'he has heard' or rewrite 'The reason for removing the spaces from the list is that...' to 'We remove the spaces because...'. Prefer shorter sentences; use periods instead of semicolons where possible. Pascal quote: longer drafts often result from lack of time to make them short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep subject near start; avoid long separations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sentences where subject and verb are separated by many words; such sentences are hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reposition or shorten intervening phrases so the subject and verb are proximal. Favor subject-verb-object style in technical writing to reduce reader effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague or conversational idioms in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conversational fillers ('Anyway', 'pretty straightforward') and vague intensifiers ('really', 'very') that obscure technical precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague terms with precise descriptions; e.g., instead of 'pretty straightforward' specify the algorithmic complexity or the key idea. Consider advice: change 'very' to 'damn' as a test for necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice where it distracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Passive voice is often flagged and should be reduced, especially when it makes exposition less direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active constructions or imperative forms where appropriate. Rule #6 suggests using 'we' to avoid passive voice, but even better can be imperative/indicative constructions (e.g., 'Replace x by 7 throughout' rather than 'We can now prove...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with the pronoun 'it' and vague referents
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences beginning 'It is unlikely...' or similar often leave the pronoun reference unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find alternative constructions that make the subject explicit to avoid ambiguous antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place commas symmetrically for parentheticals
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use commas to insert a parenthetical note, put a comma on both sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '... this node, b, is thus ...' Maintain balanced punctuation for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch placement of 'only'
rubrics_metrics.description: Misplaced 'only' changes sentence meaning and is a very common error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test different positions of 'only' to ensure the intended emphasis (examples given showing each insertion changes force). Prefer 'calculate the position of only two vertices' over 'here we only calculate...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary repetition and echoed words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not echo unusual words in unrelated passages; repetition can create unwarranted associations and monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace repeated unusual words with synonyms or restructure to avoid false connections; this also reduces typist/processing errors in technical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic precision — use words correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful with meaning distinctions (e.g., 'imply' vs 'infer', 'disinterested' vs 'uninterested').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinctions when addressing a broad audience; misuse can obscure important differences. Be cautious adopting changing usages (e.g., sentential 'hopefully') because they can distract or alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax matters — grammar reduces distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatical English avoids distracting the reader; grammar provides organizational logic for communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deliberate ungrammatical constructions in technical writing. Use standard grammar to facilitate logical clarity (case distinctions, correct pronoun forms, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositions at sentence end are acceptable when logical
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule forbidding sentence-final prepositions is called 'reactionary grammarian balderdash' and is not rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural phrasing like 'Palo Alto is a good place to live in' is often preferable to awkward rewrites; avoid needless gymnastics to obey prescriptive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place quotation marks logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Place quotation marks where they make logical sense for the content rather than following arbitrary typographer conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paul urges logical punctuation (e.g., put punctuation inside quotes only when logically part of the quoted material). Be consistent and prioritize reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerals to avoid ambiguity between word and numeral
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'one' could be a pronoun or numeral, use '1' to indicate the numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'What are we to do when x is 1?' vs confusing 'one' usage. Use numerals for clarity when context can create ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct proofs over proofs by contradiction when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs by contradiction are often less direct and can usually be replaced by clearer direct arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a direct proof if it exists (example: linear independence proofs). Proof-by-contradiction is useful for problem solving but may not produce the best exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be judicious with voice/person (we, I, imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'we' to avoid passive voice is common, but excessive use can add irrelevant dimensions; first-person singular should generally be avoided in formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider imperative or indicative moods and non-sentential labels (Consequence:, Conclusion:) to make exposition concise and less distracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not echo unusual notation or words across unrelated passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing unusual words in unrelated places causes readers to associate them and may imply links that aren't intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reusing rare terms where it can create false relationships; vary wording or restructure to prevent unintended associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting and notation: prefer readable forms
rubrics_metrics.description: When typesetting mathematics in running text, prefer readable slashed fractions and unambiguous notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use 'n(n+1)(2n+1)/3' rather than cramped stacked fractions 'n(n+1)/2n+1' that are hard to read inline. Choose notation conventions appropriate to your field (hyphenation, compound nouns) to balance readability and familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-aware hyphenation and compound usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenation choices depend on field conventions; some hyphenations that help other disciplines may be annoying in CS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'programming-language notation' versus 'programming language notation' — in CS the unhyphenated form may be clearer because terms are familiar. Apply hyphenation sparingly and with audience expectations in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation and emphasis: use exclamation points and split infinitives sensibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points should be reserved for true exclamations; blanket bans on splitting infinitives are unwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities differ on exclamation usage; consider audience and tone. Splitting infinitives can provide emphasis and avoid forced rewrites; prioritize clarity and cadence over rigid prescriptive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of automated style-tool quirks
rubrics_metrics.description: Style/diction programs may misclassify or overflag constructions (e.g., classifying any sentence beginning 'It...' or 'There...' as 'expletive', or marking passive if any passive verb appears).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how tools define categories and interpret their output accordingly; human judgment should mediate acceptance of suggestions.
